9.0: Yes, Mr. Bankes agreed, his eyes following Mr. Ramsay as he went. It was a real shame. (Lily had said something about how he frightened her—how suddenly he swung from one mood to another.) Yes, said Mr. Bankes, it was a real shame that Ramsay couldn’t manage to behave a little more like other people. (He liked Lily Briscoe; with her he could talk about Ramsay perfectly openly.) That, he said, was exactly why young people no longer read Carlyle. Here was a crusty old grumbler who flew into a temper if his porridge was cold—so why should he lecture us? That, as far as Mr. Bankes could tell, was how the young talked these days. And it was a real shame, if you happened to believe, as he did, that Carlyle was among the great teachers of humanity. Lily was embarrassed to confess she hadn’t read a line of Carlyle since her schooldays. But to her mind, Mr. Ramsay was all the more likable for believing that if his little finger hurt, the entire world must be ending. _That_ wasn’t what bothered her. After all, who could be taken in by him? He openly begged you to flatter him and admire him; nobody was fooled by his little maneuvers. What she objected to, she said, gazing after him, was how narrow he was, how blind.
9.1: “Something of a hypocrite?” offered Mr. Bankes, who was also watching Mr. Ramsay’s retreating back. Wasn’t he thinking about their friendship, and about Cam refusing to give him a flower, and about all those boys and girls—and about his own house, so comfortable, but rather quiet since his wife died? He had his work, of course. … Still, he rather hoped Lily would agree that Ramsay was, in his phrase, “something of a hypocrite.”
9.2: Lily Briscoe kept on packing her brushes away, glancing up, glancing down. When she glanced up, there he was—Mr. Ramsay—striding toward them, swinging, careless, oblivious, far away. Something of a hypocrite? she echoed. Oh no. He was the most sincere of men, the truest (here he came), the best. Yet when she looked down, she thought: he’s wrapped up in himself, he’s a tyrant, he’s unfair. And she deliberately kept her eyes lowered, because that was the only way she could keep her balance while she was staying with the Ramsays. As soon as you raised your eyes and saw them, they were flooded with what she called “being in love.” They turned into part of that unreal yet piercing and thrilling universe, the world as the eyes of love see it. The sky clung to them; the birds sang right through them. And—more thrilling still—as she watched Mr. Ramsay bearing down and then retreating, and Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window with James, and the cloud drifting and the tree bending, she felt too how life stopped being a string of small separate incidents, lived one at a time. It curled up and became whole, like a wave that carried you up with it and flung you down with it, there, crashing on the beach.
9.3: Mr. Bankes was waiting for her reply. She was on the point of saying something against Mrs. Ramsay—that she was frightening too, in her own way, overbearing, or something of the kind—when Mr. Bankes’s rapture made it quite unnecessary for her to say anything at all. And rapture was the word, given that he was over sixty, and so clean and so impersonal, and seemed to go about clothed in a white scientist’s coat. The way Lily saw him gazing at Mrs. Ramsay was a rapture that matched, she felt, the passions of dozens of young men (and perhaps Mrs. Ramsay had never inspired the passions of dozens of young men). This was love, she thought, as she made a show of shifting her canvas—love distilled and filtered, love that never tried to grasp what it loved. Like the love mathematicians have for their symbols, or poets for their phrases, it was meant to spread across the world and add to what humanity had gained. And so, indeed, it was. The world ought by all means to have shared in it, if only Mr. Bankes could have explained why that woman gave him such pleasure. Why did watching her read a fairy tale to her little boy affect him in precisely the way a solved scientific problem did? He rested, contemplating it, and felt what he felt when he had proved something absolute about how plants digest: that barbarism had been tamed, and the reign of chaos brought under control.
9.4: A rapture like this—what else could you possibly call it?—drove what she had been about to say clean out of Lily Briscoe’s head. It hadn’t mattered much; something about Mrs. Ramsay. Next to this “rapture,” this silent gaze, it faded to nothing, and she felt deeply grateful for it. Nothing consoled her like this; nothing so relieved her of life’s bewilderment, or so miraculously lifted its weight, as this sublime power, this gift from heaven. While it lasted, you would no more interrupt it than you would break up the beam of sunlight lying flat across the floor.
9.5: It helped her, it lifted her up, that people could love like this, that Mr. Bankes could feel this way about Mrs. Ramsay (she glanced over at him, lost in his thoughts). Deliberately, like a servant, she wiped her brushes one after another on a scrap of old rag. She was sheltering under the reverence that covered all women; she felt praised herself. Let him go on gazing; she would sneak a look at her painting.
9.6: She could have cried. It was bad, bad, infinitely bad! Of course, she could have done it another way. She could have thinned and faded the color and made the shapes airy and ethereal; that was how Paunceforte would have seen it. But that wasn’t how she saw it. What she saw was color burning on a steel framework; the light of a butterfly’s wing resting on a cathedral’s arches. All that was left of it was a few random marks scrawled across the canvas. And no one would ever see it; it would never even be hung. And there was Mr. Tansley, whispering in her ear, “Women can’t paint, women can’t write …”
9.7: Now it came back to her, what she had meant to say about Mrs. Ramsay. She couldn’t tell how she would have phrased it, but it would have been a criticism. The other night some bit of high-handedness had irritated her. Following the line of Mr. Bankes’s gaze toward Mrs. Ramsay, she thought that no woman could worship another woman as he worshipped her; women could only shelter together in the shade he cast over them both. Following his beam, she added her own, different ray. Mrs. Ramsay, she thought, was without question the loveliest of people (bent over her book there); perhaps the best; but also unlike the perfect form you saw before you. Yet why unlike, and unlike in what way? she wondered, scraping off her palette all those heaps of blue and green, which looked to her now like lifeless lumps of earth—though she swore that tomorrow she would breathe life into them, make them move and flow and obey her. In what way was Mrs. Ramsay different? What was the spirit in her, the essence, so that if you came across a glove tucked into the corner of a sofa you would know from its twisted finger that it was hers, beyond any doubt? For speed she was like a bird; for directness, an arrow. She was headstrong; she was commanding (naturally, Lily reminded herself, I’m thinking of how she is with women, and I’m much younger, a nobody, living off the Brompton Road). She threw open bedroom windows. She shut doors. (In this way Lily tried to get the tune of Mrs. Ramsay started in her head.) She would turn up late at night, tapping lightly on your bedroom door, wrapped in an old fur coat (that was always the setting for her beauty—hurried, but just right), and act out once again whatever it happened to be: Charles Tansley losing his umbrella; Mr. Carmichael snuffling and sniffing; Mr. Bankes announcing, “the vegetable salts are lost.” She would shape it all skillfully, even give it a malicious twist. Then she would move across to the window, pretending she had to go—it was dawn, she could see the sun coming up—and half turn back, more intimate now, yet still always laughing, to insist that she must, Minta must, all of them must marry. Because in the whole world, whatever laurels might be thrown her way (but Mrs. Ramsay didn’t care a fig about her painting), or whatever triumphs she might win (Mrs. Ramsay had probably had her share of those)—and here she grew sad and dark and returned to her chair—one thing was beyond dispute: an unmarried woman (she took Lily’s hand lightly for a moment), an unmarried woman has missed the best of life. The house seemed full of sleeping children and of Mrs. Ramsay listening; of lamps turned low and steady breathing.
9.8: Oh, but, Lily would answer, she had her father; her home; even, if she had dared say so, her painting. Yet set against the other thing, all of it seemed so slight, so virginal. Still, as the night went on and white light slipped between the curtains, and now and then some bird even chirped in the garden, she would summon up a desperate courage and argue that the universal law did not apply to her; beg to be excused from it. She liked being alone; she liked being herself; she wasn’t made for that. And then she would have to face a solemn look from eyes of matchless depth, and meet Mrs. Ramsay’s simple conviction (she was like a child now) that her dear Lily, her little Brisk, was being a fool. Then, she remembered, she had put her head in Mrs. Ramsay’s lap and laughed and laughed and laughed—laughed almost hysterically at the idea of Mrs. Ramsay ruling, with unshakable calm, over destinies she didn’t understand in the least. There she sat, simple and serious. Lily had her sense of her back now—this was the glove’s twisted finger. But what sanctuary had she broken into? At last Lily Briscoe had raised her eyes, and there was Mrs. Ramsay, with no idea at all what had made her laugh, still presiding, but with every trace of willfulness gone now. In its place was something clear, like the space the clouds finally uncover—that little patch of sky asleep beside the moon.
9.9: Was it wisdom? Was it knowledge? Or was it, yet again, beauty deceiving you, so that everything you perceived got caught halfway to the truth in a golden net? Or did she keep some secret locked inside her—the kind of secret Lily Briscoe was sure people must have, if the world was to keep going at all? Not everyone could be as haphazard, as hand-to-mouth, as she was. But if they did know, could they tell you what it was they knew? She had sat on the floor with her arms wrapped around Mrs. Ramsay’s knees, as close as she could get, smiling at the thought that Mrs. Ramsay would never know why she was pressing so hard. And she had imagined that in the chambers of this woman’s mind and heart—this woman whose body was actually touching hers—there stood, like treasures in royal tombs, tablets carved with sacred inscriptions. If you could only spell them out they would teach you everything, but they would never be offered openly, never made public. What art was there, known to love or to cunning, that would let you press on into those secret chambers? What device was there for becoming one with the thing you adored, inseparably the same, like waters poured into a single jar? Could the body do it? Or the mind, blending subtly in the brain’s intricate passages? Or the heart? Could loving, as people called it, make her and Mrs. Ramsay one? Because what she longed for was not knowledge but unity—not inscriptions on tablets, not anything that could be written in any human language, but intimacy itself, which is knowledge, she had thought, resting her head on Mrs. Ramsay’s knee.
9.10: Nothing happened. Nothing! Nothing! as she leaned her head against Mrs. Ramsay’s knee. And yet she knew that Mrs. Ramsay’s heart held stores of knowledge and wisdom. How, then, she had wondered, could you know anything at all about people, sealed up as they were? Only the way a bee does, drawn by some sweetness or sharpness in the air that can’t be touched or tasted: you hovered around the dome-shaped hive, roamed alone across the empty reaches of the air over all the countries of the world, and then hovered again around the hives with their murmurings and stirrings—the hives that were people. Mrs. Ramsay stood up. Lily stood up. Mrs. Ramsay left. For days afterward, more vividly than anything she had said, a sound of murmuring clung about her, the way after a dream you sense some subtle change in the person you dreamed about. And as she sat in the wicker armchair in the drawing-room window, she took on, in Lily’s eyes, an august shape: the shape of a dome.
9.11: Lily’s ray ran level with Mr. Bankes’s, straight to Mrs. Ramsay, sitting there reading with James at her knee. But now, while Lily was still looking, Mr. Bankes had finished. He had put his spectacles on. He had taken a step back. He had lifted his hand. He had narrowed his clear blue eyes a little—and Lily, coming to herself, saw what he was about to do and cringed, like a dog seeing a hand raised to hit it. She would have snatched her painting off the easel, but she told herself, One must. She steeled herself for the dreadful ordeal of having someone look at her picture. One must, she said, one must. And if it had to be seen, Mr. Bankes was less frightening than anyone else would be. But it was agony that any other eyes should see what her thirty-three years had left behind, the sediment of every day she had lived, mixed with something more secret than anything she had ever said or shown in all those days. And at the same time, it was enormously exciting.
9.12: Nothing could have been calmer or quieter. Mr. Bankes took out a penknife and tapped the canvas with its bone handle. What was she trying to show with that triangular purple shape, “just there?” he asked.
9.13: It was Mrs. Ramsay reading to James, she told him. She knew what he would object—that nobody could tell it was a human figure. But she hadn’t tried for a likeness, she said. So why had she put them in at all? he asked. Why indeed?—except that, since it was bright over there in that corner, she felt she needed something dark here in this one. It was simple, obvious, ordinary, but Mr. Bankes was interested. So a mother and child, he reflected—objects of universal reverence, and this mother famous for her beauty besides—could be reduced to a purple shadow without any disrespect.
9.14: But it wasn’t a picture of them, she said. Or not in the sense he meant. There were other ways, too, of honoring them. With a shadow here and a light there, for instance. That was the form her tribute took, if, as she vaguely assumed, a picture had to be a tribute. You could reduce a mother and child to a shadow without disrespect. A light here called for a shadow there. He thought it over. He was interested. He approached it scientifically, and in complete good faith. The fact was, he explained, all his prejudices ran the other way. The biggest picture in his drawing-room, which painters had admired and priced higher than what he had paid for it, showed the cherry trees in blossom along the banks of the Kennet. He had spent his honeymoon on the Kennet, he said. Lily must come and see that picture, he said. But now—he turned, spectacles raised, to examine her canvas scientifically. The question was one of how masses relate, how lights relate to shadows, and he had honestly never thought about that before; so he would like it explained to him. What, then, did she mean to make of it? And he pointed at the scene before them. She looked. She couldn’t show him what she meant to make of it; without a brush in her hand she couldn’t even see it herself. Once again she took up her old painting stance, eyes dimmed, manner absent, subduing all her impressions as a woman to something far more general. Once again she fell under the power of that vision she had once seen clearly and now had to grope for among hedges and houses and mothers and children—her picture. The question, she remembered, was how to join this mass on the right to that one on the left. She might do it by carrying the line of the branch across, like so; or she might break the empty foreground with some object (James, perhaps), like so. But the danger was that doing so might break the unity of the whole. She stopped; she didn’t want to bore him; she lifted the canvas gently off the easel.
9.15: But it had been seen; it had been taken from her. This man had shared something deeply intimate with her. She thanked Mr. Ramsay for it, and Mrs. Ramsay, and the hour and the place; she gave the world credit for a power she had never suspected it had—that you could walk away down that long gallery no longer alone, but arm in arm with someone. It was the strangest feeling in the world, and the most exhilarating. She snapped the catch of her paintbox shut, harder than she needed to, and the snap seemed to draw a circle that closed forever around the paintbox, the lawn, Mr. Bankes, and that wild villain Cam, racing past.

10.0: Cam had missed the easel by an inch. She wouldn’t stop for Mr. Bankes and Lily Briscoe, even though Mr. Bankes, who would have liked a daughter of his own, reached out his hand to her. She wouldn’t stop for her father, whom she also missed by an inch; nor for her mother, who called out “Cam! I want you a moment!” as she tore by. She was off like a bird, a bullet, an arrow—but driven by what longing, fired by whom, aimed at what, who could tell? What was it, what? Mrs. Ramsay wondered, watching her. Perhaps a vision—of a shell, a wheelbarrow, a fairyland on the other side of the hedge; or perhaps just the glory of speed; nobody knew. But when Mrs. Ramsay called “Cam!” again, the missile fell to earth in mid-flight, and Cam came dragging her feet back to her mother, plucking a leaf as she went.
10.1: What was the child dreaming about? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. She stood there so absorbed in some private thought that the message had to be given twice: go and ask Mildred whether Andrew, Miss Doyle, and Mr. Rayley are back yet. The words seemed to drop into a well whose water, clear as it was, bent things so strangely that you could watch them twisting as they sank, making heaven knows what pattern on the floor of the child’s mind. What message would Cam actually deliver to the cook? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. And in fact it was only by waiting patiently, and hearing all about an old woman in the kitchen with very red cheeks who was drinking soup out of a bowl, that Mrs. Ramsay finally set off that parrot-like instinct in her. It had caught Mildred’s words quite exactly, and could now repeat them, if you were patient, in a flat singsong. Shifting from one foot to the other, Cam recited: “No, they haven’t, and I’ve told Ellen to clear away tea.”
10.2: So Minta Doyle and Paul Rayley weren’t back yet. That could mean only one thing, Mrs. Ramsay thought. Minta must accept him, or she must refuse him. Going off for a walk after lunch like this, even with Andrew along—what else could it mean? Only that she had made up her mind, and rightly, thought Mrs. Ramsay (who was very, very fond of Minta), to accept that good fellow. He might not be brilliant. But then, Mrs. Ramsay thought—aware that James was pulling at her to make her keep reading the Fisherman and his Wife aloud—deep down she infinitely preferred dunces to clever men who wrote dissertations; men like Charles Tansley. At any rate, by now it must have happened, one way or the other.
10.3: But what she read was: “The next morning the wife woke up first. It was just dawn, and from her bed she could see the lovely countryside spread out before her. Her husband was still stretching. …”
10.4: But how could Minta turn him down now? Not if she had agreed to spend entire afternoons tramping around the countryside alone with him—for Andrew would go off after his crabs—though Nancy might have been with them. Mrs. Ramsay tried to call up the picture of them standing at the front door after lunch. There they had stood, looking up at the sky and wondering what the weather would do. And she had said, partly to cover up their shyness, partly to urge them to get going (for she was on Paul’s side),
10.5: “Not a cloud for miles in any direction,” and at that she had sensed little Charles Tansley, who had trailed out after them, snickering. But she had said it deliberately. As for whether Nancy had been there, she couldn’t be sure, going from face to face in her mind’s eye.
10.6: She read on: “ ‘Oh, wife,’ said the man, ‘why should we be King? I have no wish to be King.’ ‘Well,’ the wife answered, ‘if you won’t be King, then I will. Go to the Flounder, because I will be King.’ ”
10.7: “Either come in or go out, Cam,” she said. She knew it was only the word “Flounder” that had drawn Cam, and that any minute she would start fidgeting and fighting with James the way she always did. Off Cam shot. Relieved, Mrs. Ramsay kept reading, for she and James liked the same things and were at ease with each other.
10.8: “And when he reached the sea it was a very dark gray, and the water was heaving up from underneath and had a rotten smell. Then he went and stood beside it and said,
10.9:
‘Flounder, flounder, in the sea.
Come, I pray thee, here to me;
For my wife, good Ilsabil,
Wills not as I’d have her will.’
10.10: ‘Well, what does she want, then?’ said the Flounder.” And where had they got to by now? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. She could read and think at once with no trouble at all, for the story of the Fisherman and his Wife was like a bass line quietly accompanying a tune, now and then running up without warning into the melody. And when was she going to be told? If nothing had happened, she would have to have a serious talk with Minta. Minta simply couldn’t go tramping all over the countryside, even with Nancy along (once more she tried, and failed, to picture their backs going down the path, and to count them). She was answerable to Minta’s parents—the Owl and the Poker. Her nicknames for them flashed into her mind as she read. The Owl and the Poker—yes, they would be displeased if they heard (and they were sure to hear) that Minta, while staying with the Ramsays, had been seen et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. “He wore a wig in the House of Commons and she ably assisted him at the head of the stairs,” she said over to herself, hauling them up out of her memory with a phrase she had invented, on the way home from some party, to amuse her husband. Dear me, Mrs. Ramsay said to herself, how had those two ever produced such an unlikely daughter? This tomboy Minta, with a hole in her stocking? How did she survive in that ponderous atmosphere, where the maid was forever sweeping into a dustpan the sand the parrot had scattered, and conversation had shrunk almost entirely to that bird’s exploits—interesting, perhaps, but limited, when all was said and done? Naturally she had invited Minta to lunch, then tea, then dinner, and in the end to come and stay with them up at Finlay. That had caused some friction with the Owl, her mother, and led to more calls, and more conversation, and more sand, until, by the end of it, she had told enough lies about parrots to last a lifetime (as she had put it to her husband that night, on the way home from the party). Still, Minta came. … Yes, she had come, Mrs. Ramsay thought, feeling some thorn caught in the tangle of this thought; and when she worked it loose, she found that it was this. A woman had once accused her of “robbing her of her daughter’s affections”; and something Mrs. Doyle had said brought that accusation back to her. That she wanted to dominate, wanted to interfere, made people do what she wanted—that was the charge against her, and she thought it deeply unfair. Could she help how she looked? Nobody could say she went to any trouble to impress. She was often ashamed of how shabby she was. Nor was she domineering, nor tyrannical. It was truer where hospitals and drains and the dairy were concerned. About things like that she did feel passionately, and, given the chance, she would have liked to grab people by the scruff of the neck and make them see. Not one hospital on the whole island. It was a disgrace. Milk left on your doorstep in London that was actually brown with dirt. There ought to be a law against it. A model dairy and a hospital here—those were the two things she would have liked to do, with her own hands. But how? With all these children? Later, when they were older, maybe she would have time; once they were all at school.
10.11: Oh, but she never wanted James to get one day older, nor Cam either. These two she would have liked to keep just as they were, forever—demons of wickedness, angels of delight—and never watch them turn into long-legged monsters. Nothing could make up for that loss. Just now, when she had read James the line “and there were numbers of soldiers with kettledrums and trumpets,” and his eyes had darkened, she had thought: why should they grow up and lose all that? Of all her children he was the most gifted, the most sensitive. But every one of them, she thought, was full of promise. Prue was an absolute angel with the others, and these days, especially in the evenings, her beauty could take your breath away. Andrew—even her husband granted that he had an extraordinary gift for mathematics. And Nancy and Roger had both turned into wild creatures, running all over the countryside from morning till night. As for Rose, her mouth was too big, but she was wonderful with her hands. When they put on charades, it was Rose who made the costumes; she made everything; what she liked best was arranging things—tables, flowers, anything at all. Mrs. Ramsay didn’t like Jasper shooting birds; but that was only a phase; they all went through phases. Why, she asked, resting her chin on the top of James’s head, must they grow up so quickly? Why must they go off to school? She would have liked always to have a baby. She was never happier than with one in her arms. Then people could call her tyrannical, domineering, overbearing, whatever they pleased; she didn’t care. And as she touched his hair with her lips she thought, he will never be this happy again—but she stopped herself, remembering how angry her husband got when she said that. Still, it was true. They were happier now than they would ever be again. A tenpenny tea set could keep Cam happy for days. The moment they woke, she heard them stamping and crowing on the floor over her head. They came clattering along the passage. Then the door burst open and in they came, fresh as roses, wide-eyed, wide awake, as if coming into the dining room after breakfast—which they did every single day of their lives—were a real occasion for them. And so it went, one thing after another, all day long, until she went up to say good night and found them caught in their cots like birds netted among the cherries and raspberries, still inventing stories about some scrap of rubbish—something they had overheard, something they had found in the garden. They each had their little treasures. … And so she went downstairs and said to her husband, Why must they grow up and lose it all? They’ll never be so happy again. And he was angry. Why take such a gloomy view of life? he said. It isn’t sensible. For it was strange—and she believed it to be true—that for all his gloom and despair he was happier than she was, more hopeful on the whole. Perhaps it was that he was less exposed to human troubles. He always had his work to fall back on. Not that she was “pessimistic” herself, as he accused her of being. It was only that she thought life—and a small strip of time appeared before her eyes, her fifty years. There it lay in front of her—life. Life, she thought, but she didn’t finish the thought. She took a look at life, because she had a distinct sense of it there, something real, something private, which she shared with neither her children nor her husband. A kind of transaction went on between the two of them, with her on one side and life on the other. She was always trying to get the upper hand of it, as it was of her; and sometimes they held talks (when she sat by herself); there had been, she remembered, great scenes of reconciliation. But mostly, oddly enough, she had to admit that she felt this thing she called life to be terrible, hostile, ready to spring on you the moment you gave it the chance. There were the eternal problems: suffering; death; the poor. Even here there was always some woman dying of cancer. And yet she had told all these children, You shall go through with it. To eight people she had said it, relentlessly (and the greenhouse bill would come to fifty pounds). And for that reason, knowing what lay in store for them—love and ambition and being miserable and alone in dreary places—she often felt: Why must they grow up and lose it all? And then, brandishing her sword at life, she told herself, Nonsense. They’ll be perfectly happy. And here she was, she thought, sensing again how sinister life was, making Minta marry Paul Rayley. Because whatever she might feel about her own transaction—and she had been through things that needn’t happen to everyone (she didn’t name them, even to herself)—she was driven on, too fast, she knew, almost as if it were an escape for her as well, to declare that people must marry; people must have children.
10.12: Was she wrong about this? she asked herself, going over how she had behaved in the last week or two, and wondering whether she really had pushed Minta, who was only twenty-four, to make up her mind. It made her uneasy. Hadn’t she laughed about it? Wasn’t she forgetting, once again, how powerfully she influenced people? Marriage called for—oh, all kinds of qualities (the greenhouse bill would come to fifty pounds); and one—she didn’t need to name it—_that_ was essential; the thing she and her husband had. Did they have it?
10.13: “Then he pulled on his trousers and ran off like a madman,” she read. “But outside a great storm was raging, and the wind blew so hard he could barely keep his feet. Houses and trees were toppling, the mountains shook, rocks went rolling into the sea, the sky was pitch-black, there was thunder and lightning, and the sea rolled in with black waves as tall as church towers and mountains, every one of them crested with white foam.”
10.14: She turned the page. Only a few lines were left, so she would finish the story, even though bedtime had passed. It was getting late. She could tell from the light in the garden; and the flowers turning white and something gray in the leaves combined to wake a feeling of anxiety in her. At first she couldn’t think what it was about. Then it came to her: Paul and Minta and Andrew weren’t back. Once more she summoned up the little group on the terrace outside the hall door, standing there looking up at the sky. Andrew had taken his net and basket. That meant he meant to catch crabs and so on. That meant he would clamber out onto some rock and be cut off by the tide. Or, coming home in single file along one of those narrow paths above the cliff, one of them might slip. He would roll, and then crash. It was getting quite dark.
10.15: But she didn’t let her voice alter in the slightest as she read the story to its end. Then, closing the book, she looked into James’s eyes and added the last words as if she had invented them herself: “And there they are, living still at this very time.”
10.16: “And that’s the end,” she said. As the interest of the story faded from his eyes, she saw something else take its place: something wondering, pale, like a reflected light, that made him gaze and marvel at once. She turned and looked out across the bay, and there, sure enough, coming steadily over the waves—first two quick strokes, then one long steady stroke—was the light of the Lighthouse. It had been lit.
10.17: Any moment now he would ask her, “Are we going to the Lighthouse?” And she would have to tell him, “No, not tomorrow; your father says not.” Fortunately Mildred came in just then to fetch them, and the bustle took their minds off it. But as Mildred carried him out, he kept looking back over his shoulder, and she was sure he was thinking, we are not going to the Lighthouse tomorrow. And she thought, he will remember that for the rest of his life.
